title: Beginner making a top-down roguelike dungeon crawler for fun: which engine, free tools and AI asset workflow would you recommend?
author: Overall-Suit-5531
selftext:
Hi everyone! I'm a complete beginner at game dev and I'm doing this purely for fun. I just want to enjoy the process of making a small game, no commercial ambitions (at least for now 😄).

  The idea is a top-down roguelike dungeon crawler. Visually I'm dreaming of simple but atmospheric pixel art with a dark mood

  My situation:

  \- I'm not an artist, so I'm planning to use AI-generated assets.

  \- I'd like to stay on free tiers as much as possible, at least until I know I'm going to stick with it.

  \- The only thing I'm paying for is a Claude Pro plan, which I'd use to help me with the code.



  What I'd love to hear from you:

  1. **Engine**: I keep hearing about Unity, but it feels like it might be overkill for a small 2D pixel art game. Would you go with Godot, GameMaker, or something else? Which one works best alongside an AI coding assistant?

  2. **Art**: which free (or free-tier) tools do you use to generate pixel art sprites and tiles? How do you keep characters looking consistent? I keep watching amazin results in this sub but everyone seems to use a different combination of tools and I really don't know where to start...

  3. **Animation**: is there a beginner-friendly way to get simple walk/attack animations out of AI-generated sprites?

  4. **Workflow**: how do you combine an AI coding assistant with the engine and the art tools without getting lost?

  5. **Beginner traps**: what do you wish you'd known when you started your first project like this?

  Any tips, tool names or links to guides are really appreciated. Thanks!

comments.author: dbojan76
comments.body: godot is free and open source, so I picked that.

comments.author: Agile_Branch_8743
comments.body:
1. Godot works well for that kind of project + with Claude Code

2. Use free assets (you can hand them to Claude) to build a prototype before generating anything. Go for personal assets once the prototype has been validated. Don't burn time and ressources on making a "good-looking" vibecoded game that won't go anywhere.

5. Trying to bite more than you can chew, aka trying to make a big ambitious game before you have built and finished smaller projects.

replies.author: hateborne
replies.body:
#3 is a double edged sword but needs to be addressed. 

"Dream big, work small" was something I was told by a gent in an unrelated field. His advice was to dream of making it big, but work on small, manageable pieces to get there. You won't create the next BG3 level of "big game" overnight, but don't let that stop you from doing little by little to try to make that happen.

Additionally, "don't let perfect be the enemy of good". Polish it up, make it great, but don't waste your time/life trying to get everything absolutely perfect or you will never finish a product.

replies.author: Agile_Branch_8743
replies.body: Yes, the goal is to prove (to yourself, too) that you can finish a project and to progressively learn how to handle things. You shouldn't ideally spend too long on those learning projects and you can definitely think about where you want to go in terms of a bigger project while you work in those.

replies.author: Remarkable_Swing_709
replies.body: Agree with this. Skin and bones first, get it functioning in a crude way. Muscles next mechanics and game systems then skin with art

comments.author: Borgware
comments.body:
Engine: I would let AI write your own engine, but it also depends on your skillset. Unity is great, but its not gonna be easy to just pick up and run with it, even if you have AI. I cant really say about the other engines. Perhaps GameMaker is easier to use if you target pure 2D Pixel art game, but I havent used it myself.

Art: If you dont wanna setup something yourself, with weights from hugging face, I think pixellab is your best bet. It has a free account, but you will run out of usage pretty fast, but it will give you a sense if you want to use it further. The UI is very cumbersome, but I found it usefull if you use claude to access it. It also support animating your character. Check out there youtube page for more details.

Workflow: Getting lost? not sure what you mean by that. Working with AI is not always as structuer as tradional game dev, thats true. But you are the one driving. Personally I use Claude with project mode. Working in threads which share memory, I found it easier to work on multiple tasks that way and overhead management becomes easier. Try to use MCP or fallback to API, its always easier to automate with those tools available. Dont try to "understand" everything, if something is broken, probe it with AI to get a better understanding on whats wrong and fix it. Knowledge of what you are doing is still important though. My best suggestion is to start somewhere, get a sprite into whatever you arre building, then expand from there.

Beginners Trap: Dont try to add everything, just beacase you can. It super easy to get caught in the "Ill add this, its so easy" trap. More features wont make your game more fun, decide on what you want to do and make it small and focus on that. By small I dont mean that you game needs to be small, but you need to understand what you are aiming to achieve. To be honest, its here most get lost.

comments.author: Pik-cher
comments.body: For a first project I'd keep the scope tiny: one room, one enemy type, one weapon, and get that fun before adding anything. Godot is free and its scripting is easy for an AI assistant to help with, and you can use free asset packs as placeholders while you prototype. Generate your pixel art later, and keep one fixed palette and tile size so the AI-made pieces look consistent. Commit often so you can undo when generated code breaks something.

comments.author: jakenuts-
comments.body:
My best experiences with any AI managed project use : 

1. The latest frontier model (Fable 5.2 or Astra 6.2) to build the initial app in the desktop harnesses (Codex or Claude Desktop). You can move to less expensive models once the big challenging bits are in place.

2. Your job is not to plan the work or tell it how to build it, your job is to provide examples of what you want it to look like and act like. The best outcomes will be when you can point at an existing app or game as a reference and then give some basic changes you want to make. So "build a complete and entertaining game like Prince of Persia but with modern graphics, a western theme and playable on the web".  

3. Use one of the image generation models to build some concept graphics, it's easy to iterate on those and then hand off the vision to the coding agent. Also give your coding agent a good image generation API at the outset, and then ElevenLabs or similar APIs for music, sound effects, voiceovers. If the model has to ask you for credentials and approval every time it needs a new image it will undermine the work.

4. Some models will get lazy about gameplay specifics and the sequence of the game structure or length of the campaigns, so even though you might want to start small, explain the larger vision and how the stages build to make the game more enjoyable or you will get one level with no progression. 

Haven't built many games but several cloned web apps (which is where #2 the reference has been very successful) and some games that were great looking but short and not building toward an endpoint which is where #4 came from.

comments.author: Laperen
comments.body:
If you just want something quick, ask it to create with HTML/CSS/JS. Other than being what the AI accesses the easiest, being completely text based files allows the AI to work directly on them with zero issues. NPM also allows the AI to grab whatever libraries it needs to accomplish your task.

Using an engine with AI assisted development only makes sense for 2 reasons. You know how to fine-tune stuff yourself and have some specifics which need to be handled personally. You have target platforms which the engine is able to export to.

For art, sourcing for available assets as placeholders, or even asking the AI to do it, would be enough to get something out. You can then make more change requests from that starting point.

comments.author: jasontlouro
comments.body:
you're exactly the kind of person I'm building a tool for! Could you let me know whether [chunkyard.net](http://chunkyard.net) looks interesting to you, and why or why not? it basically is a game engine i built for 2D top-down games that makes it easier, faster, and cheaper for LLMs to build these kinds of games. It also comes with a pixel art pipeline that in my opinion makes better art than the alternatives. It's still clunky art, but it doesn't feel overly AI-y and I'd even say it's a bit endearing.

would love to hear from ya
